title: APRA warns of private credit risk to super pot
full_text:
The prudential regulator has warned of heightened risks in the nation’s $4.5 trillion retirement pot as cracks emerge in private credit.
The regulator on Wednesday said it was reviewing super trustees’ exposure to the under-pressure sector, as it proposed new rules to shore up investment oversight.
“(Private credit) is an area of heightened risk and increased level of supervision from APRA across all of our regulated entities in relation to super trustees,” David Bradbury, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority’s new deputy chair said in a media briefing.
“We are, through that supervision … seeking to understand the extent of exposures that trustees may have to various parts of the private credit ecosystem.” It comes weeks after the corporate watchdog warned of cracks emerging in private credit, as fears grow of a looming crisis in the non-bank lending market.
A central part of the regulator’s supervision is making sure trustees recognise their accountability to members in investment governance, Mr Bradbury added.
His comments came a day after Australia’s biggest non-bank corporate lender, Metrics Credit Partners, suspended redemptions from two of its funds and put a 90-day pause on lending. The Australian understands Metrics has been included in the Australian Securities & Investments Commission’s second tranche of surveillance in the sector that has taken place in recent months, with findings to be released as soon as next month. Metrics was also part of ASIC’s first round of surveillance of the sector last year.
While ASIC wades through funds’ opaque exposures in unlisted assets, including private credit, the prudential regulator is focused on super trustees’ monitoring of investments in the wake of the Shield and First Guardian failures. APRA on Wednesday opened fresh consultation with the industry on the need for stronger investment governance.
The regulator is proposing new rules that would force trustees to enforce limits for higher-risk investments; better manage investment-related conflicts; and improve investment oversight capabilities and resources.
“Trustees are ultimately accountable for the investments they make available to members,” Mr Bradbury said.
“The failures of Shield and First Guardian demonstrate the serious harm that can occur when members accumulate concentrated holdings in poor or unsuitable investment options.” APRA also fired a none-too-subtle warning shot over the sector’s lax standards, proposing executive pay rules currently imposed on larger trustees could be extended to smaller operators.
These rules allow for clawback provisions on executive bonuses and deferrals on pay.
The Financial Services Council urged APRA to tread carefully. “Codified hard investment limits into what APRA determines are ‘high risk’ investments or requiring trustees to apply a performance test to individual options, without accounting for the role of financial advice and an individual’s assets outside of superannuation, could have a material impact on Australians’ accumulation and management of wealth,” FSC chief executive Blake Briggs said.
